issues.legal_issue: A homestead tenant who ceases to hold raiyati land loses the special protection afforded to the homestead of a raiyat, and the tenancy is thereafter governed by ordinary tenancy rules.
material_facts: The predecessor of the defendants had a homestead on the disputed plots and held agricultural land as a raiyat.
The courts found that he was dispossessed of his entire agricultural holding under a statutory proceeding.
The plaintiff company sued for recovery of possession of the homestead plots.
issues.conclusion: The defendants could no longer rely on the homestead protection in Section 78 of the Chhota Nagpur Tenancy Act; their tenancy was governed by the Transfer of Property Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 78 of the Chhota Nagpur Tenancy Act protects a raiyat's homestead while the tenant continues to hold raiyati land. The Court adopted the view in Joy Chand v. Bhutnath Khan and Secretary of State v. Babu Ben Prasad that the protection ends when the tenant parts with the raiyati land; the homestead tenancy then becomes subject to ordinary incidents of tenancy. The Court applied this principle to the findings concerning dispossession under Section 50 of the Act.

predicates.possession_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking possession of land occupied by another.
predicates.homestead_held_separately: The occupant held the homestead otherwise than as part of the occupant's raiyati holding.
predicates.raiyati_land_lost: The occupant ceased to hold the agricultural land that gave the occupant raiyat status.
predicates.homestead_protection_ends_and_ordinary_t: The occupant no longer receives special protection for the homestead and the tenancy is governed by ordinary tenancy rules.

issues.definition: When a possession suit concerns a separately held homestead and its occupant has lost the raiyati land, the special homestead protection ends and ordinary tenancy rules apply.

issues.legal_issue: A prior determination of a tenant's interest in a homestead does not bar reconsideration when the tenant's interest has materially changed after losing the raiyati land on which the earlier determination depended.
material_facts: An earlier suit had determined the predecessor's interest in the disputed plots while they were treated as part of his agricultural holding.
The predecessor was later found to have lost his entire agricultural holding.
The later suit concerned his successors' rights in the homestead plots after that loss.
issues.conclusion: The earlier findings did not prevent consideration of the defendants' interest after the change in circumstances; the change in the nature of that interest supported treating the earlier determination as no bar.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a prior determination does not operate as res judicata where a material change in circumstances means the right or interest now in issue is different. It treated the continuing availability of the protection under Section 78 of the Chhota Nagpur Tenancy Act as the test of whether the defendants' interest had changed, relying on Joy Chand v. Bhutnath Khan and Secretary of State v. Babu Ben Prasad for the scope of that protection.

predicates.possession_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking possession of land occupied by another.
predicates.prior_determination_of_interest: An earlier proceeding determined the occupant's interest in the land now in dispute.
predicates.material_change_in_interest: A later event changed the nature of the occupant's interest relevant to the later dispute.
predicates.prior_determination_does_not_bar_reconsi: The earlier determination does not prevent the court from deciding the occupant's interest as changed by the later event.

issues.definition: If a possession suit follows an earlier determination of an interest and a later event materially changes that interest, the earlier determination does not bar reconsideration of the changed interest.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a plaintiff may maintain a possession suit after statutory vesting depends on whether the plaintiff retained an interest in the disputed land, and that question must be determined rather than treated as irrelevant.
material_facts: The trial court found that the intermediary interests of the plaintiff company and its lessor had vested in the State under land reform legislation.
The first appellate court did not decide whether the plaintiff company retained an interest after vesting.
The High Court treated vesting as irrelevant because it considered the tenancy governed by the Transfer of Property Act.
The plaintiff company had obtained a decree for ejectment in the first appellate court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had to determine whether the land vested and whether the plaintiff company consequently ceased to have an interest. The Supreme Court remanded the case for that finding: if the plaintiff had no subsisting interest, the suit was to be dismissed; otherwise, the ejectment decree was to be affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: The plaintiff's entitlement to recover possession depends on its subsisting interest in the land. The Court held that vesting under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 could affect maintainability even though the tenancy was governed by the Transfer of Property Act, and directed the High Court to determine the factual effect of vesting.

predicates.possession_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking possession of land occupied by another.
predicates.statutory_vesting_may_have_ended_plainti: A statutory vesting may have left the claimant without an interest in the land at issue.
predicates.remand_for_interest_finding_and_conditio: The case must be remanded to determine whether the claimant retained an interest, with dismissal if none remained and affirmance of the possession decree if an interest remained.

issues.definition: When statutory vesting may have ended a claimant's interest in land sought in a possession suit, the case is remanded to determine that interest and dispose of the suit accordingly.
